A lots of docs were created about the package sync (scope of and implemented in this PR). User requirements were very high level at the start: only what was in issue description of #118 and maybe in another, old, high-level doc that lists all functionalities of pc-switcher. Don't bother searching for it.
Along the way, while responding to your analysis questions and to the many questions that came up during implementation, testing and review (still in progress), the requirements became finer but the decisions we made have spread around a myriad of docs, code comments, ADR, ...
I asked you in another session to reconstruct a user requirements document. This gave "docs/planning/Package sync requirements.md". That's not what I wanted.

So let's take a step back. What is a "user requirements document" for you?
For me, it is NOT a list of 100's of separate rules that are impossible to reconstruct mentally (for a human; I don't know about you but I doubt) into a vision of how the product should do, look like, behave. The 100's of rules written like a lawbook are the conversion of the "user requirements document" into hard rules that the implementation can be checked against.
For me, user requirements are more prose, maybe with diagrams or sketches, that explain the intent of a product and how it should work and behave. Use-cases can be a good way to express (a big) part of user requirements, but not everything can nor should be formulated as use case.
What do you propose as structure and how do we get there? I absolutely want the reconstruct a high level user requirements doc like I describe it, because with all documentation spread over a lot of places and mostly as small individual decisions without a vision of the whole nor of how the individual rules hang together, it has become impossible for me, nor for any reviewer or tester, human or AI agent, to
- understand the product and the logic that we need and decided upon, after all back-and-forth decisions;
- verify if the implementation covers those real user's needs/requests.

I want to be able to review a (rather high-level, but concrete) document that I understand, approve it, and then let a reviewer critically check if the implementation and the tests cover the requirements.

Do you agree? Challenge me if there are points you disagree with or if this is a bad idea anyway.

PS Don't throw away the detailed articles of "docs/planning/Package sync requirements.md" if they are still valuable.

PPS I just glanced through them and spotted immediately a first problem with ambiguous phrasing. A requirements doc should be written in a way that it is clear and unambiguous.
PKG-FR-MACHINE-SPECIFIC: "offered again on that machine. The mark MUST be local to that machine": "THAT" machine is very unclear. What we decided: the decision that something is machine-specific, is noted in a decision file on the machine that holds the "something". This will be often the target machine, even though pc-switcher is launched on the source machine and the question is presented on the source machine and the decision is made on the source machine.
Example: Source machine does not have package P, target machine has package P. The user is asked on the source machine if package P should be removed from the target machine. The user says "skip always". This decision tells that package P is "machine specific" for the target machine, so the decision is stored there.
I'll start by understanding what exists today before proposing a structure.

content.text:
I read the existing doc and mapped what feeds it. Here's my position before I propose anything.

## What a user requirements document is, for me

It's the document that makes a reader able to **predict** the product. Test: hand someone who finished it a situation the doc never mentions, and they get the answer roughly right. A lawbook can't do that — it can only *check* an answer, never generate one. So I agree with you, and I'd go further: `Package sync requirements.md` isn't wrong, it's **mislabelled**. It's a conformance checklist — genuinely good at that job, 122 articles, each individually defensible — and it should keep existing under an honest name, demoted to derived.

You're also right that it's unreadable as a whole, and the reason is structural, not stylistic: the articles are sorted by *mechanism* (apt, snap, flatpak) when the thing that actually makes package sync comprehensible is that it's **one model with four instantiations**, and each manager's oddities are forced by what that ecosystem actually is. apt is where every hard problem lives; snap is "one store so no origin question, but exact revision because `~/snap/<rev>` is in the data path"; flatpak is "apt's origin problem again, but no distribution remote exists"; manual installs is "nothing can reproduce it, so you write the recipe once and the recipe travels". Nobody can extract that from 122 alphabetised MUSTs, but with it, most of the 122 become predictable.

## Where I disagree with you

**Use cases are the wrong primary spine here.** This product has one actor, one trigger, and one use case — "sync before I switch machines" — and package sync is a phase inside it. Formal use-case templates (actor / precondition / main flow / alternates) would fragment one coherent flow into dozens of near-identical stubs and add bureaucracy without adding predictive power. What carries the meaning is a **walkthrough of one run** plus **worked scenarios with real names** ("you installed `gh` from GitHub's repo on P17 — here's what XPS13 sees, here's the screen, here's why it asks about the package and not the repository"). Scenarios illustrate the model; they don't replace it. That's the one point in your framing I'd change.

**And your ambiguity example isn't a phrasing problem — it's a missing-vocabulary problem.** `PKG-FR-MACHINE-SPECIFIC` says "that machine" twice with no antecedent because the doc has never named the distinction between the two *roles* (source/target, per run) and the machine that **holds** the item. The real rule — install/change diffs are held by the source and recorded there; removal diffs are held by the target and recorded there, written remotely — is unstatable without that noun. Fix the glossary and the whole class of ambiguity closes; then re-audit the 122 against it. Prose alone wouldn't have caught it.

Four decisions I'd rather not guess at.

Noted on the preview — that was the traceability map drawn in the wrong direction, and you're right to push back: the narrative body must carry **no PKG-IDs at all** or it reads like the lawbook again. The map belongs in the articles doc (each article points up to its narrative section), plus one appendix table there for coverage checking. The narrative stays clean prose.

input.content:
# Reconstruct a high-level user requirements document for package sync

## Context

Package sync (issue #118, PR #206, phase 02) started from a one-line requirement and grew its real requirements incrementally, through analysis questions, implementation choices, review findings and UAT prep. Those decisions now live in ADR-020 (D-01..D-42), `.planning/phases/02-package-management-sync/` (CONTEXT, DISCUSSION-LOG, two SPECs, #208 design, UAT runbook, review reports), `docs/system/`, `docs/jobs/`, module docstrings, and `docs/planning/Package sync requirements.md`.

That last file is 122 normative articles (`PKG-FR-*`, `PKG-NG-*`), each individually defensible. It is a good conformance checklist and a bad requirements document: sorted by mechanism rather than by model, it can check an answer but never generate one. Nobody — user, human reviewer, or agent — can read it and predict what the product does in a situation it does not name. So the product cannot be reviewed as a whole, and the implementation cannot be judged against a stated intent.

Outcome wanted: one document the user reads end to end, understands, corrects and approves. After approval it becomes the reference for a staged validation — first the 122 articles against it, then code, tests and the remaining docs against the articles.

## What gets built

Two documents with distinct jobs and an explicit precedence between them.

`docs/planning/Package sync - user requirements.md` (new) — narrative prose plus mermaid diagrams. Authoritative for intent. No requirement IDs anywhere in the body. Rationale is written inline as prose ("…because two branches of one application install side by side"), not as footnote lines.

`docs/planning/Package sync - conformance criteria.md` (renamed from `Package sync requirements.md`, content preserved) — the 122 articles, demoted to a derived checkable decomposition. Gains a header stating that the narrative rules on intent, per-section pointers up to the narrative section each block decomposes, and one appendix table mapping every ID to its narrative section so coverage is mechanically checkable.

Names are proposed, not fixed: path plus filename must convey topic ("Package sync") and document type ("user requirements" / "conformance criteria"). Easy to change at review.

## Narrative outline

The spine is the model first, managers as deltas from it. This is the structural claim worth approving or rejecting before any prose is written: package sync is **one model with four instantiations**, and each manager's oddities are forced by what that ecosystem actually is — apt carries every hard problem, snap has one store but revision-numbered data paths, flatpak repeats apt's origin problem with no distribution remote, manual installs cannot be reproduced at all so the user writes the recipe.

1. What package sync is for — the switching workflow, why software must land before user data, why this is convergence and not mirroring, what the four jobs cover, and what is explicitly not theirs (application data).
2. Vocabulary — source and target as per-run roles; the machine that **holds** an item; item, diff, decision, derived mechanism, origin/vendor, machine-specific, snippet, flatpak scope, snap revision and channel. Two lines each. This section is what closes the `PKG-FR-MACHINE-SPECIFIC` "that machine" class of ambiguity at the root.
3. The model in one page — the five ideas everything else follows from: the source states intent and the target's own managers do the work; identity includes provenance where an ecosystem has more than one vendor; the user is asked about software and plumbing is derived from that answer; nothing is touched before the review returns and removals are never a default; a manager's failure is its own and the run continues. Mermaid: the shared plan → review → apply pipeline.
4. One run, start to finish — narrated walkthrough with all four jobs enabled: preconditions, job order, the snapd refresh pause, what each job reads, the Ubuntu Pro gate, what the screens actually show, what apply does, what the report says at the end. This is the artifact that currently does not exist anywhere and the one that makes the 122 articles cohere.
5. Decisions and their memory — apply / not this time / never here, and where "here" is. Carries the worked example: source lacks package P, target has it, the question is asked on the source, "skip always" is recorded **on the target**, because the target holds the item. Why marks never travel while the snippet registry does. What cannot be marked, and why.
6. apt — the full model. Installing (keep the existing mermaid decision tree), origin replication and the post-convergence verification, removals, version and vendor divergence, holds, collateral damage, repositories/keys/pins as derived plumbing, the transactional `/etc/apt` group, Ubuntu Pro and ESM.
7. snap — deltas only: one store so no origin question; exact revision and channel, and why (`~/snap/<rev>` in the data path, so folder_sync is only correct when both machines match); refresh pause; sideloads; holds.
8. flatpak — deltas only: scope + full ref as identity; remotes carry trust and not just a URL; no distribution remote exists; repoint versus delete; filters do not travel; masks.
9. Manual installs — deltas only: detection is source-side; three resolutions; the snippet as an opaque recipe run as the target user with no stdin; the registry travels and its overwrite gate; install-only, never removal.
10. When something goes wrong — per-item failures, derived failures charged to the packages that needed them, what a skipped job means, rehearsal, no terminal.
11. What it deliberately does not do — the non-goals as prose with each cost named.
12. Open questions — genuinely undecided items, carried forward.

Target ≤700 lines including diagrams. A section that balloons past its share is a signal the model is wrong, not that the section needs more room.

## How the reconstruction runs

Stage 1 — behaviour ledger, scratchpad only, nothing committed. Code first: read `jobs/apt_sync.py`, `snap_sync.py`, `flatpak_sync.py`, `manual_installs_sync.py`, the shared core under `jobs/packages/` (`sync_core.py`, `review.py`, `state.py`, `items.py`, `probes.py`, `apt_policy.py`), plus the wiring in `orchestrator.py`, `folder_sync.py`, `cli.py` and `default-config.yaml`. Record every user-visible behaviour with `file:line`. Then read ADR-020, `02-CONTEXT.md`, `02-DISCUSSION-LOG.md`, `02-SPEC-package-review-model.md`, `02-SPEC-snap-flatpak-derivation.md`, `02-208-HOLD-MASK-REPLICATION.md` and `02-UAT-01-RUNBOOK.md` for rationale and intent only — what the code does comes from the code.

Stage 2 — divergence report, delivered alongside the draft as a separate short list, never resolved silently. Seeds already spotted by exploration and to be confirmed against the source in Stage 1, not asserted before then: `ProbeFailed` appears to propagate out of the orchestrator's `except Exception` arm and end the whole run, which would contradict `PKG-FR-OUTCOME-FAILED`; `PCSWITCHER_PACKAGE_REVIEW_AUTOMATION` appears to bypass all prompting while still reporting `was_interactive=True`, so permanent marks and snippets get written on a path absent from `--help`, the config schema and every doc; `manual_installs_sync` appears to be missing from the job-order validation that covers the other three; the per-job passwordless-sudo preconditions (apt both machines, snap both, flatpak target-only and only for system scope, manual none) are stated nowhere in the articles; dry run appears to still show and answer the review.

Stage 3 — write the narrative. Every behavioural sentence traceable to a ledger entry.

Stage 4, after the narrative is approved — rename and demote the articles doc, add the precedence header, the per-section up-pointers and the ID-to-section appendix, and fix inbound links.

Stage 5, after the narrative is approved — ambiguity audit of all 122 articles against the new glossary: undefined antecedents, unnamed roles, terms used two ways. Delivered as a findings list with proposed rewrites for approval, applied only after.

Stages 4 and 5 are deliberately gated on approval so the narrative is judged on its own before anything else moves.

## Files

Create `docs/planning/Package sync - user requirements.md`.

`git mv docs/planning/Package sync requirements.md` to `docs/planning/Package sync - conformance criteria.md`, then edit its header and add the traceability appendix.

Fix inbound links — grep for `Package%20sync%20requirements` and `Package sync requirements` across `docs/` and `.planning/`; known referrers include `docs/README.md`, `docs/adr/_index.md`, `docs/adr/adr-020-declarative-package-convergence.md`, `docs/planning/High level requirements.md`, `docs/jobs/package-sync.md`, `docs/system/package-sync.md`, `.planning/phases/02-package-management-sync/02-SCENARIO-COVERAGE.md`.

Scratchpad, not committed: behaviour ledger and divergence report under `/tmp/claude-1000/-home-janfr-dev-pc-switcher/0c0e36c3-689a-4554-be65-d4a075a59e88/scratchpad/`.

No source code changes.

Predictive test — the real one. Nobody — user, human reviewer, or agent — can read it and predict what the product does in a situation it does not name. Two documents with distinct jobs and an explicit precedence between them.

## Narrative outline

The spine is the model first, managers as deltas from it. This is the structural claim worth approving or rejecting before any prose is written: package sync is **one model with four instantiations**, and each manager's oddities are forced by what that ecosystem actually is — apt carries every hard problem, snap has one store but revision-numbered data paths, flatpak repeats apt's origin problem with no distribution remote, manual installs cannot be reproduced at all so the user writes the recipe.

1. What package sync is for — the switching workflow, why software must land before user data, why this is convergence and not mirroring, what the four jobs cover, and what is explicitly not theirs (application data).
2. Vocabulary — source and target as per-run roles; the machine that **holds** an item; item, diff, decision, derived mechanism, origin/vendor, machine-specific, snippet, flatpak scope, snap revision and channel. Two lines each. This section is what closes the `PKG-FR-MACHINE-SPECIFIC` "that machine" class of ambiguity at the root.
3. The model in one page — the five ideas everything else follows from: the source states intent and the target's own managers do the work; identity includes provenance where an ecosystem has more than one vendor; the user is asked about software and plumbing is derived from that answer; nothing is touched before the review returns and removals are never a default; a manager's failure is its own and the run continues. Mermaid: the shared plan → review → apply pipeline.
4. One run, start to finish — narrated walkthrough with all four jobs enabled: preconditions, job order, the snapd refresh pause, what each job reads, the Ubuntu Pro gate, what the screens actually show, what apply does, what the report says at the end. This is the artifact that currently does not exist anywhere and the one that makes the 122 articles cohere.
5. Decisions and their memory — apply / not this time / never here, and where "here" is. Carries the worked example: source lacks package P, target has it, the question is asked on the source, "skip always" is recorded **on the target**, because the target holds the item. Why marks never travel while the snippet registry does. What cannot be marked, and why.

It is a good conformance checklist and a bad requirements document: sorted by mechanism rather than by model, it can check an answer but never generate one. Nobody — user, human reviewer, or agent — can read it and predict what the product does in a situation it does not name. So the product cannot be reviewed as a whole, and the implementation cannot be judged against a stated intent.

Outcome wanted: one document the user reads end to end, understands, corrects and approves. After approval it becomes the reference for a staged validation — first the 122 articles against it, then code, tests and the remaining docs against the articles.

## What gets built

Two documents with distinct jobs and an explicit precedence between them.

`docs/planning/Package sync - user requirements.md` (new) — narrative prose plus mermaid diagrams. Authoritative for intent. No requirement IDs anywhere in the body. Rationale is written inline as prose ("…because two branches of one application install side by side"), not as footnote lines.

`docs/planning/Package sync - conformance criteria.md` (renamed from `Package sync requirements.md`, content preserved) — the 122 articles, demoted to a derived checkable decomposition. Gains a header stating that the narrative rules on intent, per-section pointers up to the narrative section each block decomposes, and one appendix table mapping every ID to its narrative section so coverage is mechanically checkable.

Names are proposed, not fixed: path plus filename must convey topic ("Package sync") and document type ("user requirements" / "conformance criteria"). Easy to change at review.

## Narrative outline

The spine is the model first, managers as deltas from it. The structural claim worth approving or rejecting before any prose is written: there is one convergence model, it applies to software a package manager on the target can be told to install, and each manager's oddities are forced by what that ecosystem actually is — apt carries every hard problem, snap has one store but revision-numbered data paths, flatpak repeats apt's origin problem with no distribution remote.

Everything else is the complement — software no manager can reproduce — and that is deliberately not treated as one thing. It has at least four kinds with genuinely separate detection and handoff logic: a hand-downloaded `.deb` (apt knows the name but no configured repository offers that version, so `apt_sync` drops it and hands it over); software under `/usr/local` and `/opt` that no package owns (script installs, tarballs); a sideloaded snap; and a flatpak installed from a local bundle or from a remote that no longer exists. The only thing the four share is the **install snippet** as their reproduction mechanism. Today only the first two are handled: sideloaded snaps are detected, excluded, and then replicated by nobody, and the flatpak equivalent is unverified — both #221, deferred out of this phase. The narrative states that as a current gap rather than describing intended behaviour as if it shipped.

The narrative is organised by kind of software, never by the internal job decomposition. Which code unit owns which kind is implementation and is expected to change (#220 would likely resplit it). The two things at this level that *are* user-visible: which kinds of software the user chooses to sync, and that software must land before user data.

1. What package sync is for — the switching workflow, why software must land before user data, why this is convergence and not mirroring, which kinds of software are in scope and which the user opts into individually, and what is explicitly out of scope (application data).
2. Vocabulary — source and target as per-run roles; the machine that **holds** an item; item, diff, decision, derived mechanism, origin/vendor, machine-specific, snippet, flatpak scope, snap revision and channel. Two lines each. This section is what closes the `PKG-FR-MACHINE-SPECIFIC` "that machine" class of ambiguity at the root.
3. The model in one page — the five ideas everything else follows from: the source states intent and the target's own managers do the work; identity includes provenance where an ecosystem has more than one vendor; the user is asked about software and plumbing is derived from that answer; consent precedes every change, with questions bundled into one review per manager as a strong preference rather than an obligation, since an approved action can establish facts that were unknowable before it landed and a further question then is correct — and removals are never a default; a manager's failure is its own and the run continues. Mermaid: the shared plan → review → apply pipeline.
4. One run, start to finish — narrated walkthrough with everything enabled: preconditions, what runs before what, the snapd refresh pause, what is read from each machine, the Ubuntu Pro gate, what the screens actually show, what applying does, what the report says at the end. This is the artifact that currently does not exist anywhere and the one that makes the 122 articles cohere.
5. Decisions and their memory — apply / not this time / never here, and where "here" is. Carries the worked example: source lacks package P, target has it, the question is asked on the source, "skip always" is recorded **on the target**, because the target holds the item. Why marks never travel while the snippet registry does. What cannot be marked, and why.
6. apt — the full model. Installing (keep the existing mermaid decision tree), origin replication and the post-convergence verification, removals, version and vendor divergence, holds, collateral damage, repositories/keys/pins as derived plumbing, the transactional `/etc/apt` group, Ubuntu Pro and ESM.
7. snap — deltas only: one store so no origin question; exact revision and channel, and why (`~/snap/<rev>` in the data path, so folder_sync is only correct when both machines match); refresh pause; holds; and the sideload exclusion, described as a handoff that does not yet have a receiver (§9).
8. flatpak — deltas only: scope + full ref as identity; remotes carry trust and not just a URL; no distribution remote exists; repoint versus delete; filters do not travel; masks.
9. Software no manager can reproduce — structured by kind, not as one lump: the hand-downloaded `.deb`; unowned software under `/usr/local` and `/opt`; the sideloaded snap and the flatpak bundle or dead-remote ref, both stated as the #221 gap they currently are. Then what they share: detection is source-side; three resolutions; the snippet as an opaque recipe run as the target user with no stdin; the registry travels and its overwrite gate; install-only, never removal.
10. When something goes wrong — per-item failures, derived failures charged to the packages that needed them, what a skipped job means, rehearsal, no terminal.
11. What it deliberately does not do — the non-goals as prose with each cost named.
12. Open questions — genuinely undecided items, carried forward.

Target ≤700 lines including diagrams. A section that balloons past its share is a signal the model is wrong, not that the section needs more room.

## How the reconstruction runs

Stage 1 — behaviour ledger, written to `.planning/phases/02-package-management-sync/02-BEHAVIOUR-LEDGER.md` and committed. It is the evidence behind every sentence in the narrative and the input to the later validation passes, so it lives in git next to `02-REVIEW.md` and `02-VERIFICATION.md`, not in a temp directory. Code first: read `jobs/apt_sync.py`, `snap_sync.py`, `flatpak_sync.py`, `manual_installs_sync.py`, the shared core under `jobs/packages/` (`sync_core.py`, `review.py`, `state.py`, `items.py`, `probes.py`, `apt_policy.py`), plus the wiring in `orchestrator.py`, `folder_sync.py`, `cli.py` and `default-config.yaml`. Record every user-visible behaviour with `file:line`. Then read ADR-020, `02-CONTEXT.md`, `02-DISCUSSION-LOG.md`, `02-SPEC-package-review-model.md`, `02-SPEC-snap-flatpak-derivation.md`, `02-208-HOLD-MASK-REPLICATION.md` and `02-UAT-01-RUNBOOK.md` for rationale and intent only — what the code does comes from the code.

Stage 2 — divergence report, written to `.planning/phases/02-package-management-sync/02-DIVERGENCES.md` and delivered alongside the draft as a separate list, never resolved silently. Seeds already spotted by exploration and to be confirmed against the source in Stage 1, not asserted before then: `ProbeFailed` appears to propagate out of the orchestrator's `except Exception` arm and end the whole run, which would contradict `PKG-FR-OUTCOME-FAILED`; `PCSWITCHER_PACKAGE_REVIEW_AUTOMATION` appears to bypass all prompting while still reporting `was_interactive=True`, so permanent marks and snippets get written on a path absent from `--help`, the config schema and every doc; `manual_installs_sync` appears to be missing from the job-order validation that covers the other three; the per-job passwordless-sudo preconditions (apt both machines, snap both, flatpak target-only and only for system scope, manual none) are stated nowhere in the articles; dry run appears to still show and answer the review; and `PKG-NG-SIDELOAD` claims sideloaded snaps "cannot be reproduced" as an accepted cost, which #221 contradicts — a snippet running `snap install --dangerous` reproduces one, so this is an unbuilt handoff, not a law of nature.

Stage 3 — write the narrative. Every behavioural sentence traceable to a ledger entry.

Stage 4, after the narrative is approved — rename and demote the articles doc, add the precedence header, the per-section up-pointers and the ID-to-section appendix, and fix inbound links.

Stage 5, after the narrative is approved — ambiguity audit of all 122 articles against the new glossary: undefined antecedents, unnamed roles, terms used two ways. Delivered as a findings list with proposed rewrites for approval, applied only after.

Stages 4 and 5 are deliberately gated on approval so the narrative is judged on its own before anything else moves.

## Files

Create `docs/planning/Package sync - user requirements.md`.

`git mv docs/planning/Package sync requirements.md` to `docs/planning/Package sync - conformance criteria.md`, then edit its header and add the traceability appendix.

Fix inbound links — grep for `Package%20sync%20requirements` and `Package sync requirements` across `docs/` and `.planning/`; known referrers include `docs/README.md`, `docs/adr/_index.md`, `docs/adr/adr-020-declarative-package-convergence.md`, `docs/planning/High level requirements.md`, `docs/jobs/package-sync.md`, `docs/system/package-sync.md`, `.planning/phases/02-package-management-sync/02-SCENARIO-COVERAGE.md`.

Create `.planning/phases/02-package-management-sync/02-BEHAVIOUR-LEDGER.md` and `02-DIVERGENCES.md`, both committed.

No source code changes.

## Verification

Predictive test — the real one. Take the 13 lettered divergence scenarios in `02-UAT-01-RUNBOOK.md` §4 (apt installs, apt removal with manual collateral, report-only group, repository deletion, pin deletion, flatpak remote deletion, repository conflict, snap divergence, flatpak ref divergence, flatpak remote repoint, unreproducible item, snippet-registry overwrite, apt hold). For each, check that the expected behaviour is derivable from the narrative alone by someone who has not read the articles. Scenarios that are not derivable are gaps in the narrative and get fixed; report the result explicitly rather than claiming coverage.

Coverage — every one of the 122 IDs maps to exactly one narrative section. Orphans in either direction (an article with no home, a narrative section decomposed by no article) are reported as findings, not papered over.

Traceability — every behavioural statement in the narrative has a ledger entry with `file:line`. Statements that only have a decision-doc source and no code backing are marked in the divergence report rather than stated as fact.

House style — no `---` separators, no bold-as-heading, no mid-sentence hard wrapping, diagrams in mermaid, links relative and resolving.

## Out of scope

No code, test or behaviour changes. No resolution of the divergences found — they are reported for the user to rule on. No edits to ADR-020 or the phase artifacts.

Any artifact that later work depends on — behaviour ledgers, divergence reports, extraction/analysis output, findings lists — must be written into the repo (e.g. the GSD phase dir alongside `02-REVIEW.md`) and committed. The session scratchpad under `/tmp` is only for throwaway intermediate files.

101	# concrete action" checkable rather than left to each job's own wording.
102	# `_build_review_groups` falls back to the bare `DiffAction` value for any (item_class,
103	# action) pair not listed here, so a missing vocabulary entry degrades to a plain verb
104	# instead of silently dropping the group (the backstop this plan requires: every diff
105	# class the engine produces gets SOME review presentation).
106	#
107	# `APT_SOURCE`/`APT_PIN` are deliberately absent: their only surviving direction is
108	# removal, and ADR-020 D-07 route that through `AptSyncJob`'s own
109	# `REPO_REMOVAL_REVIEW_ACTION` groups, which supply their own title and verb before this
110	# table is ever consulted.
111	_ACTION_VOCABULARY: dict[tuple[ItemClass, DiffAction], str] = {
112	    (ItemClass.APT_PACKAGE, DiffAction.INSTALL): "install",
113	    (ItemClass.APT_PACKAGE, DiffAction.CHANGE): "change",
114	    (ItemClass.APT_PACKAGE, DiffAction.REMOVE): "remove",
115	    (ItemClass.APT_PACKAGE, DiffAction.REPORT_ONLY): "report",
116	    # `/etc/apt/apt.conf.d` is the one non-package class reviewed in all three directions
117	    # (ADR-020 D-37), so all three need a verb — without them a config file reads
118	    # "Install/Change/Remove apt packages", which is wrong about both the verb and the
119	    # thing. Paired with `_ITEM_CLASS_NOUN` below, which fixes the second half.
120	    (ItemClass.APT_CONFIG, DiffAction.INSTALL): "add",
121	    (ItemClass.APT_CONFIG, DiffAction.CHANGE): "update",
122	    (ItemClass.APT_CONFIG, DiffAction.REMOVE): "delete",
123	    (ItemClass.SNAP_CHANNEL, DiffAction.CHANGE): "retrack",
124	    # Block-state membership items (#208): the add direction reads "hold"/"mask" and the
125	    # remove direction "unhold"/"unmask", never "install"/"remove". `_build_review_groups`
126	    # keys the group title AND every entry's action_label off this table by the group's own
127	    # item class, so a hold/mask item never displays under an "Install/Remove packages"
128	    # group even when it shares a `DiffAction` with a package.
129	    (ItemClass.APT_HOLD, DiffAction.INSTALL): "hold",
130	    (ItemClass.APT_HOLD, DiffAction.REMOVE): "unhold",
131	    (ItemClass.SNAP_HOLD, DiffAction.INSTALL): "hold",
132	    (ItemClass.SNAP_HOLD, DiffAction.REMOVE): "unhold",
133	    (ItemClass.FLATPAK_MASK, DiffAction.INSTALL): "mask",
134	    (ItemClass.FLATPAK_MASK, DiffAction.REMOVE): "unmask",
135	}
136	
137	# What a group's title calls the things it lists, when they are not packages. A verb alone
138	# cannot make an apt-config title true: the title reads "<verb> <manager> packages", so
139	# every `/etc/apt/apt.conf.d` group would still end in "apt packages". Hold and mask items
140	# are absent on purpose — they ARE about packages, so the default noun is already right.
141	_ITEM_CLASS_NOUN: dict[ItemClass, str] = {
142	    ItemClass.APT_CONFIG: "apt configuration files",
143	}
144	
145	# Fixed emission order for review groups: install before change before remove keeps
146	# the most common/least-destructive action first; report_only trails since it needs a
147	# decision but implies no direct converge verb.
148	_ACTION_ORDER: tuple[DiffAction, ...] = (
149	    DiffAction.INSTALL,
150	    DiffAction.CHANGE,
151	    DiffAction.REMOVE,
152	    DiffAction.REPORT_ONLY,
153	)
154	
155	
156	class PackageSyncJob(SyncJob):
157	    """Shared plan()/apply() pipeline every package-manager job subclasses.
158	
159	    Deliberately carries NO `name` ClassVar: `Orchestrator._resolve_sync_job_class` scans
160	    a job module's attributes for a `SyncJob` subclass whose `name` matches the module
161	    name (`getattr(attr, "name", None) == job_name`), so an abstract base without `name`
162	    is invisible to job discovery even when a concrete subclass imports it into scope.
163	    """
164	
165	    manager_id: ClassVar[str]
166	
167	    def __init__(self, context: JobContext) -> None:
168	        super().__init__(context)
169	        self._accepted_plan: PackagePlan | None = None
170	        self._accepted_outcome: ReviewOutcome | None = None
171	        # Both machines' decision files as the last `plan()` call read them, so a subclass
172	        # that EXTENDS the base plan (only `apt_sync`, with its collateral and repo diffs)
173	        # can run `_drop_inert_diffs` over its own extra diffs without a second pair of
174	        # remote reads. Re-assigned on every `plan()`, never cached across calls.
175	        self._plan_decisions: tuple[Mapping[str, DecisionEntry], Mapping[str, DecisionEntry]] = ({}, {})
176	
177	    # -- Abstract hooks subclasses implement -------------------------------------------
178	
179	    @abstractmethod
180	    async def plan(self) -> PackagePlan:
181	        """Capture, diff and build this job's review groups. Read-only.
182	
183	        Every manager owns its own: what a diff even IS differs per ecosystem (apt has
184	        pins, holds and transaction collateral; snap converges a revision and a channel;
185	        flatpak carries scope and remote trust; a manual install has a snippet or has
186	        nothing). There is no diff shape all four share, so there is no base
187	        implementation to inherit — only the pieces below, which every implementation
188	        does use: `filter_inert` on the way in, `_drop_inert_diffs` on the way out, and
189	        `_build_review_groups` at the end.
190	
191	        Nothing here may mutate either machine: a job plans and reviews before it
192	        converges, so `plan()` runs before the user has approved anything. An
193	        implementation MUST load both machines' decision files and filter each side's
194	        items through its OWN file (D-08), then run the resulting diffs through
195	        `_drop_inert_diffs` to catch the recorded items no input-side filter can see —
196	        the block-state membership items (`apt:hold:`, `snap:hold:`) and anything else
197	        whose identity is derived rather than carried on an input item.
198	        """
199	        ...
200	
201	    @abstractmethod
202	    async def converge(self, diff: ItemDiff) -> CommandResult:
203	        """Apply one approved diff on the target.
204	
205	        May raise `ConvergeItemFailed` to refuse the item without even attempting the
206	        mutating command (e.g. a transaction-safety guard); otherwise returns the
207	        `CommandResult` of the converge command, whose `.success` decides pass/fail.
208	        Called for every APPLY-decided diff whose action is `INSTALL`, `REMOVE` or
209	        `CHANGE` — `REPORT_ONLY` diffs never reach this hook (see `apply()`).
210	        """
211	        ...
212	
213	    @staticmethod
214	    def _decision_holder_is_source(action: DiffAction) -> bool:
215	        """D-08a's holder rule: an `INSTALL`/`CHANGE` diff is source-held (the source has
216	        the item, or the version it should converge to), a `REMOVE` diff target-held.
217	
218	        One definition shared by the WRITE path (`_record_permanent_skips` picks the
219	        executor whose file gets the entry) and the READ path (`_drop_inert_diffs` picks
220	        the file to look the item up in), so the machine a skip-always lands on is by
221	        construction the machine it is read back from.
222	        """
223	        return action in (DiffAction.INSTALL, DiffAction.CHANGE)
224	
225	    def _drop_inert_diffs(
226	        self,
227	        diffs: Sequence[ItemDiff],
228	        source_decisions: Mapping[str, DecisionEntry],
229	        target_decisions: Mapping[str, DecisionEntry],
230	    ) -> tuple[ItemDiff, ...]:
231	        """Drop every diff whose `item_id` is recorded "skip always" on the machine that
232	        holds it (D-08/D-08a) — the post-diff counterpart to `filter_inert`.
233	
234	        Required for any diff whose identity does not exist on an input item and so cannot
235	        be filtered at the diff-input boundary: the block-state membership items
236	        (`apt:hold:<name>`, `snap:hold:<name>`) are derived from hold-set membership, and
237	        apt's repo/collateral diffs are derived from directory digests. Without this pass
238	        a permanently-declined hold is re-emitted every run — and in the add direction it
239	        comes back default-checked, so a bulk accept applies the very hold the user
240	        declined.
241	
242	        `REPORT_ONLY` diffs pass through untouched: they carry no converge verb, so
243	        `_record_permanent_skips` never records one and there is no holder to match.
244	        """
245	        kept: list[ItemDiff] = []
246	        for diff in diffs:
247	            if diff.action not in (DiffAction.INSTALL, DiffAction.CHANGE, DiffAction.REMOVE):
248	                kept.append(diff)
249	                continue
250	            holder = source_decisions if self._decision_holder_is_source(diff.action) else target_decisions
251	            if diff.item_id not in holder:
252	                kept.append(diff)
253	        return tuple(kept)
254	
255	    def _build_review_groups(self, diffs: Sequence[ItemDiff]) -> tuple[ReviewGroup, ...]:
256	        """One `ReviewGroup` per `(action, item_class)` present in `diffs`, keyed on
257	        `(manager, action)` for the reviewer's removal-direction test (D-24) so removals
258	        never share a group with installs. The title's verb and every entry's
259	        `action_label` come from `_ACTION_VOCABULARY`, keyed by the group's own item
260	        class — so a block-state membership item (`apt:hold:`, `snap:hold:`,
261	        `flatpak:mask:`) whose add direction shares the `INSTALL` action with a package
262	        still reads "Hold/Mask ..." rather than displaying under "Install packages"
263	        (#208). `_ITEM_CLASS_NOUN` does the same for the title's OBJECT, so the one
264	        reviewed class that is not a package — `/etc/apt/apt.conf.d` — is not announced as
265	        one. Grouping by item class as well as action is what keeps that verb correct
266	        when one action mixes item classes (e.g. apt package INSTALL alongside apt hold
267	        INSTALL); the group's `action` value stays the raw `DiffAction` so add-direction
268	        stays default-checked and remove-direction lands in its own unticked group.
269	
270	        Emission order: `_ACTION_ORDER` (install, change, remove, report) outer, and
271	        within one action the item classes in first-seen order — which, because
272	        `_diff_apt_packages` emits package diffs before hold diffs, keeps a package group
273	        ahead of its hold group.
274	        """
275	        by_key: dict[tuple[DiffAction, ItemClass], list[ItemDiff]] = {}
276	        class_order: dict[DiffAction, list[ItemClass]] = {}
277	        for diff in diffs:
278	            key = (diff.action, diff.item_class)
279	            if key not in by_key:
280	                by_key[key] = []
281	                class_order.setdefault(diff.action, []).append(diff.item_class)
282	            by_key[key].append(diff)
283	
284	        groups: list[ReviewGroup] = []
285	        for action in _ACTION_ORDER:
286	            for item_class in class_order.get(action, []):
287	                entries = by_key[(action, item_class)]
288	                # REPORT_ONLY has no more-specific per-item-class meaning for any current
289	                # manager (IN-01): fall back to "report" rather than the raw enum value
290	                # ("report_only"), which read awkwardly in review text like "Report_only
291	                # flatpak packages". Every other action still falls back to its own
292	                # `action.value`, unchanged.
293	                default_verb = "report" if action == DiffAction.REPORT_ONLY else action.value
294	                verb = _ACTION_VOCABULARY.get((item_class, action), default_verb)
295	                noun = _ITEM_CLASS_NOUN.get(item_class, f"{self.manager_id} packages")
296	                groups.append(
297	                    ReviewGroup(
298	                        manager=self.manager_id,
299	                        action=action.value,
300	                        title=f"{verb.capitalize()} {noun}",
301	                        entries=tuple(
302	                            ReviewEntry(item_id=diff.item_id, label=diff.label, action_label=verb, detail=diff.detail)
303	                            for diff in entries
304	                        ),
305	                    )
306	                )
307	        return tuple(groups)
308	
309	    # -- plan() / accept_review() / apply() / execute() -------------------------------
310	
311	    def accept_review(self, plan: PackagePlan, outcome: ReviewOutcome) -> None:
312	        """Store this job's plan plus the outcome its own review returned."""
313	        self._accepted_plan = plan
314	        self._accepted_outcome = outcome
315	
316	    async def after_review(self) -> None:
317	        """Hook: work that must run AFTER this job's review returns but BEFORE any
318	        mutation on the target (`apply()`).
319	
320	        No-op on the base — the three managers that produce no unreproducible items (apt,
321	        snap, flatpak) need nothing between review and converge. Only `manual_installs_sync`
322	        overrides it (D-23): it pushes the freshly reconciled install-snippet registry to
323	        the target here, so a snippet the user authored during THIS run's review is on the
324	        target before `apply()` replays it. Keeping the hook on the base leaves `execute()`
325	        the single source of the plan/review/apply order rather than each manager
326	        re-deriving it.
327	        """
328	        return
329	
330	    async def apply(self) -> None:
331	        """Converge every APPLY-decided diff from the accepted plan, one item at a time.
332	
333	        Per-item detail at `LogLevel.FULL`, one `LogLevel.INFO` summary line per job
334	        (ADR-010). A per-item failure (`ConvergeItemFailed`, or a converge command that
335	        exits non-zero) is caught, logged with its stderr as structured context, and
336	        collected — the loop always completes (D-27) — then `PackageItemFailures` is
337	        raised once, after the loop, if anything failed OR anything is left unresolved
338	        (D-21) — even when `total` is zero, since an interactive run whose ONLY diffs
339	        were unreproducible items never has any INSTALL/CHANGE/REMOVE work to do, and
340	        must still fail if one of them ended up unresolved.
341	
342	        Dry-run (ADR-014): each intended action is logged at FULL with a `[dry-run] `
343	        prefix, carrying the diff's own detail, and no converge command is ever issued.
344	
345	        `REPORT_ONLY` diffs are excluded here regardless of decision: they imply no
346	        converge verb (D-25's version-mismatch, repo-unavailable, origin-mismatch and
347	        unreproducible classes are informational), so `converge()` is never called
348	        for one even if something recorded `APPLY` against it.
349	
350	        Before converging anything, `_record_permanent_skips` persists a `DecisionEntry`
351	        for every `SKIP_ALWAYS`-decided item (D-08). The `_finalize_unreproducible` hook
352	        then persists this run's authored snippets and unreproducible-item skip-always
353	        decisions (D-20/D-21/D-23); it is a no-op on the base and only
354	        `manual_installs_sync` implements it (D-18), but the call site stays here so both
355	        run before any converge, independent of whether this run applies anything else
356	        (a run with zero installs but one newly-authored snippet still records it). The
357	        `_unresolved_as_failures` hook (also no-op on the base, overridden only by
358	        `manual_installs_sync`) supplies the genuinely-undecided items that fail an
359	        interactive run — which is why `total == 0` can still raise `PackageItemFailures`.
360	        """
361	        assert self._accepted_plan is not None
362	        assert self._accepted_outcome is not None
363	        plan = self._accepted_plan
364	        outcome = self._accepted_outcome
365	        decisions = outcome.decisions
366	
367	        await self._record_permanent_skips(plan, decisions)
368	        await self._finalize_unreproducible(plan, outcome)
369	
370	        apply_diffs = [
371	            diff
372	            for diff in plan.diffs
373	            if decisions.get(diff.item_id) == Decision.APPLY and diff.action != DiffAction.REPORT_ONLY
374	        ]
375	        prefix = "[dry-run] " if self.context.dry_run else ""
376	        total = len(apply_diffs)
377	
378	        failures: list[tuple[ItemDiff, str]] = []
379	        if total == 0:
380	            self._log(Host.TARGET, LogLevel.INFO, f"{prefix}No {self.manager_id} changes to apply")
381	            self._report_progress(ProgressUpdate(percent=100))
382	        else:
383	            self._log(Host.TARGET, LogLevel.INFO, f"{prefix}Applying {total} {self.manager_id} change(s)")
384	
385	            for index, diff in enumerate(apply_diffs):
386	                if self.context.dry_run:
387	                    # The detail belongs on the line, not only in the review panel: a
388	                    # dry run never renders that panel, and ADR-014 makes the preview
389	                    # the whole report. Without it the preview says strictly less about
390	                    # an item than the interactive review does.
391	                    detail = f" — {diff.detail}" if diff.detail else ""
392	                    self._log(Host.TARGET, LogLevel.FULL, f"{prefix}Would {diff.action.value} {diff.label}{detail}")
393	                else:
394	                    await self._converge_one(diff, failures)
395	                self._report_progress(ProgressUpdate(percent=int((index + 1) / total * 100)))
396	
397	            succeeded = total - len(failures)
398	            self._log(
399	                Host.TARGET,
400	                LogLevel.INFO,
401	                f"{prefix}{succeeded}/{total} {self.manager_id} change(s) applied",
402	            )
403	
404	        all_failures = [*failures, *self._unresolved_as_failures(plan, outcome)]
405	        if all_failures:
406	            summary = "; ".join(f"{diff.label}: {stderr.strip()}" for diff, stderr in all_failures)
407	            self._log(
408	                Host.TARGET,
409	                LogLevel.INFO,
410	                f"{len(all_failures)} {self.manager_id} item(s) failed: {summary}",
411	            )
412	            raise PackageItemFailures(self.manager_id, all_failures)
413	
414	    def _unresolved_as_failures(self, plan: PackagePlan, outcome: ReviewOutcome) -> list[tuple[ItemDiff, str]]:
415	        """Hook: this job's genuinely-undecided items that fail an interactive run (D-27).
416	
417	        No-op on the base — it returns an empty list, so the three managers that produce
418	        no unreproducible items (apt, snap, flatpak) never fail on this basis. Only
419	        `manual_installs_sync` overrides it (D-18/D-21): an unreproducible item left with
420	        neither a snippet nor a recorded decision after an interactive review fails the
421	        job. The D-27 converge-failure contract in `apply()` is unchanged — converge
422	        failures fail the job regardless of what this hook returns.
423	        """
424	        return []
425	
426	    async def _finalize_unreproducible(self, plan: PackagePlan, outcome: ReviewOutcome) -> None:
427	        """Hook: persist this job's unreproducible-item snippet authoring and skip-always
428	        decisions (D-20/D-21/D-23).
429	
430	        No-op on the base — only `manual_installs_sync` produces unreproducible items
431	        (D-18), and it overrides this hook with the real persistence; the three managers
432	        that never do inherit this no-op so the base `apply()` stays generic.
433	        """
434	        return
435	
436	    async def _record_permanent_skips(self, plan: PackagePlan, decisions: Mapping[str, Decision]) -> None:
437	        """Persist a `DecisionEntry` for every `SKIP_ALWAYS`-decided, actionable diff.
438	
439	        D-08a decides WHICH machine's file gets the entry by which machine HOLDS the
440	        item: `INSTALL`/`CHANGE` diffs are source-held (the source has the item, or the
441	        version it should converge to), so they record on `self.source`; `REMOVE` diffs
442	        are target-held (only the target has the item), so they record on `self.target`
443	        — through the remote executor, never a local write (ADR-002).
444	
445	        `REPORT_ONLY` diffs are skipped: they carry no converge verb (version-mismatch,
446	        repo-unavailable, origin-mismatch and unreproducible are informational only), so
447	        there is no "holder" for D-08a to record against.
448	
449	        Two guards, both required before anything is ever written: never for a
450	        non-interactive outcome (D-26 — nothing is recorded permanently when nothing
451	        was actually decided by a human), and never during a dry run (ADR-014 — a
452	        rehearsal must leave no trace).
453	        """
454	        if self.context.dry_run or not self._accepted_outcome_was_interactive():
455	            return
456	
457	        recorded_at = datetime.now(UTC).isoformat()
458	        for diff in plan.diffs:
459	            if decisions.get(diff.item_id) != Decision.SKIP_ALWAYS:
460	                continue
461	            if diff.action not in (DiffAction.INSTALL, DiffAction.CHANGE, DiffAction.REMOVE):
462	                continue
463	
464	            executor = self.source if self._decision_holder_is_source(diff.action) else self.target
465	            await DecisionFile(self.manager_id, executor).record(
466	                DecisionEntry(
467	                    item_id=diff.item_id,
468	                    item_class=diff.item_class,
469	                    label=diff.label,
470	                    reason=None,
471	                    recorded_at=recorded_at,
472	                )
473	            )
474	
475	    def _accepted_outcome_was_interactive(self) -> bool:
476	        assert self._accepted_outcome is not None
477	        return self._accepted_outcome.was_interactive
478	
479	    async def _converge_one(self, diff: ItemDiff, failures: list[tuple[ItemDiff, str]]) -> None:
480	        try:
481	            result = await self.converge(diff)
482	        except ConvergeItemFailed as exc:
483	            failures.append((diff, str(exc)))
484	            self._log(Host.TARGET, LogLevel.ERROR, f"{diff.label} failed: {exc}", stderr=str(exc))
485	            return
486	
487	        if result.success:
488	            self._log(Host.TARGET, LogLevel.FULL, f"{diff.action.value} {diff.label}")
489	        else:
490	            failures.append((diff, result.stderr))
491	            self._log(
492	                Host.TARGET,
493	                LogLevel.ERROR,
494	                f"{diff.label} failed: {result.stderr.strip()}",
495	                stderr=result.stderr,
496	            )
497	
498	    async def execute(self) -> None:
499	        """The `SyncJob` entry point the orchestrator's sequential job loop calls.
500	
501	        Self-contained (D-24): plan this job's diffs, review its own groups through the
502	        injected `JobContext.reviewer`, accept the outcome, run the `after_review()` hook
503	        (the seam where `manual_installs_sync` pushes its snippet registry, D-23), then
504	        apply. No component outside the job owns its review, and no fallback applies diffs
505	        that never came back from one — a missing reviewer fails loudly here rather than
506	        silently skipping the review and converging unreviewed diffs (T-02-38).
507	
508	        A `plan()` failure propagates unchanged, so the orchestrator's per-job exception
509	        handling attributes it to this job's own `JobResult`.
510	
511	        A non-interactive run with a non-empty plan raises `JobSkipped`: D-26 forces every
512	        item to SKIP_ONCE with nobody present to decide, so continuing would converge
513	        nothing and report SUCCESS. It is raised before `after_review()`, so
514	        `manual_installs_sync` does not push its registry either, and before any mutating
515	        command, as `JobSkipped` requires. An EMPTY plan on the same path stays SUCCESS —
516	        the target already matches the source, which is the goal met.
517	        """
518	        assert self.context.reviewer is not None, (
519	            f"{self.manager_id} sync has no reviewer; the orchestrator must inject one "
520	            "through JobContext.reviewer before execute()."
521	        )
522	        plan = await self.plan()
523	        outcome = await self.context.reviewer.review(plan.groups)
524	        if plan.groups and not outcome.was_interactive:
525	            raise JobSkipped(
526	                self.name,
527	                f"non-interactive run left every {self.manager_id} review item undecided",
528	            )
529	        self.accept_review(plan, outcome)
530	        await self.after_review()
531	        await self.apply()
532

1	"""Machine-local decision store: the ONLY pc-switcher state deliberately per-machine
2	and never synced (D-08, D-08a, D-09).
3	
4	An entry recorded here means "inert on THIS machine in both roles": not pushed when
5	this machine is the source, not installed or removed when this machine is the target.
6	D-19's whole argument for scanning aggressively — a finding produces noise exactly
7	once, then never again — only holds if this durability is real.
8	
9	Which machine's file gets an entry follows which machine HOLDS the item (D-08a): a
10	source-held item declined during review is recorded on the source, a target-held
11	item whose removal is declined is recorded on the target. Because the file is
12	machine-local, the write must land on the correct END of the connection — on the
13	target this means going through the remote executor, never a local `pathlib` write
14	(ADR-002: the target has no direct filesystem access from here). `DecisionFile` takes
15	an `Executor` at construction and issues every read/write as a shell command through
16	it, so the SAME code path serves both roles; there is no separate "local write"
17	branch to accidentally use for the target.
18	
19	Decision files live at `~/.config/pc-switcher/<manager>.decisions.yaml`, next to
20	`config.yaml` (D-09) — one file per manager, so `apt_sync`'s decisions never collide
21	with `snap_sync`'s. The directory portion is derived from `config_sync.CONFIG_REMOTE_DIR`
22	rather than a second hardcoded literal (the CR-01 precedent `folder_sync` already
23	follows for its own tool-state filter token).
24	
25	This module also owns `SnippetRegistry` (D-20, D-23): the SHARED, synced counterpart to

262	@dataclass(frozen=True)
263	class Snippet:
264	    """One recorded install snippet (D-20): an opaque shell command that reproduces an
265	    item no package manager can install on its own.
266

269	    NEVER inspected by this dataclass or its callers beyond being replayed byte-for-byte.
270	    """

272	    item_id: str
273	    label: str
274	    body: str
275	    authored_at: str  # ISO-8601 UTC
276	    authored_on: str  # hostname of the machine the snippet was authored on
277

279	def _serialize_snippets(entries: Mapping[str, Snippet]) -> str:
280	    """Render `entries` as the snippet-registry YAML body, header regenerated fresh."""
281	    snippets = {
282	        item_id: {
283	            "label": entry.label,

305	    entries: dict[str, Snippet] = {}
306	    for item_id, fields in snippets.items():

317	def load_snippets_from_text(raw: str) -> dict[str, Snippet]:
318	    """Parse snippet-registry file content into `{item_id: Snippet}`, degrading to an
319	    empty mapping on empty or malformed input (the same rule `SnippetRegistry.load`

323	    bytes `_push_snippet_registry` is about to `send_file` to the target — when deciding

327	    """

345	    `SnippetRegistry(self.source)` to read/write the source's own copy — the reproducibility
346	    authority `plan()` classifies against (corrected D-23), and where a freshly authored
347	    snippet is recorded before that run's push carries it to the target — or
348	    `SnippetRegistry(self.target)` to read the target's copy at converge time, after this
349	    run's push has already placed it there.
350	    """
351	
352	    def __init__(self, executor: Executor) -> None:
353	        self._executor = executor
354	        # shlex.quote() is a no-op for this fixed, already-shell-safe relpath, applied
355	        # anyway per T-02-01 (ASVS V5) — see `DecisionFile.__init__`'s identical
356	        # reasoning for why it stays OUTSIDE the `~/` prefix.
357	        self._path_expr = f"~/{shlex.quote(SNIPPET_REGISTRY_RELPATH)}"
358	        self._display_path = f"~/{SNIPPET_REGISTRY_RELPATH}"
359	
360	    async def load(self) -> dict[str, Snippet]:
361	        """Read every snippet, or an empty mapping if the registry is absent, empty or
362	        malformed — mirrors `DecisionFile.load`'s degrade rule; only the malformed case
363	        logs a WARNING naming the path.
364	        """
365	        result = await self._executor.run_command(f"cat {self._path_expr} 2>/dev/null")
366	        if not result.success or not result.stdout.strip():
367	            return {}
368	
369	        try:
370	            return _deserialize_snippets(result.stdout)
371	        except (yaml.YAMLError, KeyError, TypeError, ValueError, AttributeError) as exc:
372	            _logger.warning(
373	                "Malformed snippet registry %s (%s); treating as no snippets",
374	                self._display_path,
375	                exc,
376	            )
377	            return {}
378	
379	    async def get(self, item_id: str) -> Snippet | None:
380	        """The snippet registered for `item_id`, or `None` if there is none."""
381	        entries = await self.load()
382	        return entries.get(item_id)
383	
384	    async def add(self, snippet: Snippet) -> None:
385	        """Merge `snippet` into the registry by `item_id` (last write wins) and write
386	        atomically — the identical `mkdir --parents && printf ... > tmp && mv --force` shape
387	        `DecisionFile.record` uses, so an interrupted write can never leave a truncated
388	        file.
389	        """
390	        entries = await self.load()
391	        entries[snippet.item_id] = snippet
392	        content = _serialize_snippets(entries)
393	
394	        dir_relpath = shlex.quote(_DECISION_DIR_RELPATH)
395	        tmp_expr = f"{self._path_expr}.pcswitcher-tmp"
396	        cmd = (
397	            f"mkdir --parents ~/{dir_relpath} && "
398	            f"printf '%s' {shlex.quote(content)} > {tmp_expr} && "
399	            f"mv --force {tmp_expr} {self._path_expr}"
400	        )
401	        result = await self._executor.run_command(
402	            cmd, mutates=f"record install snippet for {snippet.label} in {self._display_path}"
403	        )
404	        if not result.success:
405	            raise RuntimeError(
406	                f"failed to add snippet for {snippet.item_id!r} in {self._display_path}: {result.stderr.strip()}"
407	            )
408	
409	    async def replay(self, item_id: str, executor: RemoteExecutor) -> CommandResult:
410	        """Replay the snippet registered for `item_id` against `executor` (always the
411	        TARGET in practice) as an opaque blob (D-20): the body is never parsed,
412	        templated or inspected, only quoted.
413	
414	        Runs as `bash -c <shlex.quote(body)>` — the same build-a-command,
415	        pass-content-as-an-argv-quoted-string shape `vscode_state_sync.target_sql_command`
416	        uses for SQL — with `login_shell=False`, since a snippet is a fixed shell script,
417	        not something that needs the user's `~/.profile` sourced. No stdin is ever
418	        supplied (`pcswitcher.executor.Process` documents this is intentional), so a
419	        snippet expecting a prompt fails rather than hanging the sync. The returned
420	        `CommandResult`'s exit code alone decides success — never raises for "no
421	        snippet registered", instead returning a failed `CommandResult` so a stale plan
422	        (the registry changed between `plan()` and `apply()`) is a per-item failure
423	        like any other, not a crash that stops the whole job (D-27).
424	
425	        The exact `bash -c <quoted body>` command is what `--confirm-each-command` shows:
426	        an opaque snippet is the one thing in a sync whose content pc-switcher cannot vouch
427	        for, so it is displayed verbatim before it runs.
428	        """
429	        snippet = await self.get(item_id)
430	        if snippet is None:
431	            return CommandResult(exit_code=1, stdout="", stderr=f"no snippet registered for {item_id!r}")
432	
433	        cmd = f"bash -c {shlex.quote(snippet.body)}"
434	        return await executor.run_command(
435	            cmd, login_shell=False, mutates=f"replay install snippet for {snippet.label}"
436	        )

1	"""The fail-fast boundary for package-manager READS (ADR-022).
2	
3	Free functions, not a base class: ADR-020 D-15/D-16 keeps the four package jobs
4	independent, and a guard every job needs is exactly the kind of thing a shared base class
5	would smuggle a manager's assumptions into. `apt_policy.py` is the precedent.
6	
7	The distinction this module exists to hold is the one in ADR-022: a tool that ANSWERED —
8	including answering "nothing" — produced data, and data is this project's business to
9	handle. A tool that did not answer produced nothing, and reading its silence as data is how
10	an empty manifest becomes "that machine has nothing" and every item on the other machine
11	becomes a removal proposal. That second case fails the job, once, naming the command.
12	
13	What counts as "did not answer" is per command and is NOT inferable from the exit code
14	alone — measured, in a stock `ubuntu:24.04` container unless noted:
15	
16	* `apt-mark showmanual`/`showhold`, `apt-cache policy`, `flatpak list`/`remotes`/`mask`,
17	  `snap list --all`: a real failure exits non-zero (apt 100, flatpak 1, snap 1), and an
18	  empty answer exits 0. Their exit code IS the discriminator.
19	* `snap list --all` with zero snaps installed exits 0, prints the "No snaps are installed
20	  yet." hint on stderr, and leaves stdout empty (measured against the real `snap` binary
21	  driven by a stub snapd socket answering `/v2/snaps` with an empty result). Empty stdout
22	  is a legitimate answer, never a failure.
23	* `apt-cache policy` exits 0 for a name it has never heard of, so a non-zero exit is never
24	  a statement about a package — which is why apt additionally passes `answers`.
25	* `dpkg --search` over paths that are deliberately expected to be unowned, and
26	  `sha256sum <glob>` over a glob that legitimately matches nothing, BOTH exit non-zero in
27	  their normal case. Those callers must not use this guard; see ADR-022.
28	"""
29	
30	from __future__ import annotations
31	
32	from pcswitcher.models import CommandResult, Host
33	
34	__all__ = ["ProbeFailed", "require_answer"]
35	
36	
37	class ProbeFailed(RuntimeError):
38	    """A package-manager READ this run's correctness depends on did not answer at all.
39	
40	    Deliberately NOT a `ConvergeItemFailed`. That type means "what we asked for is wrong",
41	    which is under our control, belongs to one item, and lets the run continue (ADR-020
42	    D-27). This one means the tool or the machine is broken — a transient network failure,
43	    a package-manager lock, an interrupted dpkg, a daemon that is not running — which no
44	    item's own state explains. It escapes the per-item loops on purpose, so the run fails
45	    ONCE naming the command that failed rather than N times naming N items.
46	
47	    One type across all four package jobs, because the caller that must react to it is the
48	    orchestrator, which has no reason to care which manager's read went dark.
49	    """
50	
51	
52	def require_answer(
53	    command: str,
54	    result: CommandResult,
55	    host: Host,
56	    *,
57	    answers: int | None = None,
58	    answer_noun: str = "answer",
59	) -> None:
60	    """Refuse to read a probe's silence as an answer about the things it was asked about.
61	
62	    Raises `ProbeFailed` on a NON-ZERO EXIT, and — only when the caller passes `answers` —
63	    on `answers == 0`. `answers` is the number of parsed answers the caller KNOWS was owed;
64	    pass it only where at least one answer is genuinely guaranteed, never as a blanket
65	    "output was empty" check, because for most of these commands an empty answer is a
66	    legitimate state of the machine.
67	
68	    The `answers` half is a JUDGEMENT, recorded as one: a probe that answered "I know none
69	    of these" and a probe that died both print nothing, and the output alone cannot
70	    separate them. It is resolved toward failing fast because the alternative misattributes
71	    an environment failure to every item, and because a set the tool knows nothing about is
72	    a set nothing could be done with anyway. A per-name absence INSIDE an answered probe is
73	    left alone: that is the tool saying it does not know that one name, which is evidence
74	    about that one request.
75	    """
76	    if result.success and answers != 0:
77	        return
78	    condition = (
79	        f"exited {result.exit_code}"
80	        if not result.success
81	        else f"exited 0 but printed no {answer_noun}, so its output is not an answer"
82	    )
83	    detail = f": {result.stderr.strip()}" if result.stderr.strip() else ""
84	    raise ProbeFailed(f"probe on the {host.value} did not answer — `{command}` {condition}{detail}")

2	
3	Two jobs ask apt three different questions off the same command, and all three need the
4	same version-table walk to answer them: `apt_sync` asks what repository an INSTALLED
5	package came from (C26's source-removal impact, and ADR-020 D-34's provenance comparison)
6	and what repository the version the TARGET would install comes from (D-34's origin
7	classification); `manual_installs_sync` asks whether a package on the SOURCE came from any
8	repository at all (D-18).
9	
10	The installed and the candidate row are DIFFERENT rows and answer different questions —
11	apt happily offers a package from one vendor while a second vendor's copy is the one
12	installed — so the two live behind one walker (`_origins_by_package`) that differs only in
13	which version row it collects from.
14	
15	Shared here rather than duplicated per job, and here rather than on `PackageSyncJob`.
16	D-15 forbids one manager's diff on the shared BASE CLASS (adr-020, "Job split into four
17	jobs"): this module defines no class and sits in no job's MRO, so the other three managers
18	inherit nothing from it. `manual_installs_sync`'s own rule — it never imports `apt_sync`
19	(D-18) — also still holds, since both jobs import a third module instead. What is NOT
20	worth duplicating is a stateful indentation walker with three separate subtle rules
21	(installed-block tracking, eight-space origin rows, the `/var/lib/dpkg/status` pseudo
22	-origin); `apt_sync._parse_pin_file`'s docstring records what one earlier duplicated
23	parser of this size already cost this project.
24	"""
25	
26	from __future__ import annotations

28	from collections.abc import Sequence

30	__all__ = [
31	    "candidate_origins_by_package",
32	    "installed_origins_by_package",
33	    "normalise_repo_uri",
34	    "packages_installed_from_no_repository",
35	]

37	# dpkg's own record of an installed package. It appears as an origin row on every
38	# installed version and is not a repository.
39	_DPKG_STATUS = "/var/lib/dpkg/status"

41	
42	def normalise_repo_uri(uri: str) -> str:
43	    """A repository URI reduced to the shape `apt-cache policy` prints in its version
44	    table: apt strips the trailing slash a source file may carry
45	    (`https://packages.microsoft.com/repos/azure-cli/` -> `.../azure-cli`), so comparing
46	    the two forms verbatim would miss every repo written with one.
47	    """
48	    return uri.rstrip("/")

51	def installed_origins_by_package(policy_output: str) -> dict[str, frozenset[str]]:
52	    """Parse a batched `apt-cache policy <name...>` run into `{package: origin URIs of
53	    its INSTALLED version}` (C26).
54	
55	    `apt-cache policy`'s version table marks the installed version with a leading `***`
56	    and indents each of that version's origins by eight spaces as
57	    `<priority> <uri> <suite>/<component> <arch> Packages`. Only the installed version's
58	    origins count: another version row may list a repository that merely *offers* the
59	    package (Ubuntu's archive offers `gh` too), which is not the repository the machine is
60	    actually tracking. `/var/lib/dpkg/status` is dpkg's own record of the installed
61	    package, not a repository, and is skipped — every installed package lists it.
62	
63	    A key MEANS apt printed a block for that name; the value means what apt said about it.
64	    The two are deliberately separable, because a package installed from a local `.deb`
65	    reaches an empty origin set while a name apt has never heard of reaches no key at all,
66	    and the difference is the difference between "apt says no repository supplies this" and
67	    "apt said nothing" — including the case where the whole command failed and produced no
68	    output. `packages_installed_from_no_repository` may only indict the first.
69	    """
70	    return _origins_by_package(policy_output, of_candidate=False)
71	
72	
73	def candidate_origins_by_package(policy_output: str) -> dict[str, frozenset[str]]:
74	    """Parse a batched `apt-cache policy <name...>` run into `{package: origin URIs of the
75	    version apt WOULD install}` (ADR-020 D-34).
76	
77	    Not the same rows as `installed_origins_by_package`, and the difference is the whole
78	    point: a machine can have vendor A's copy installed while apt's candidate is vendor B's,
79	    and matching a package by name alone reads the second as "the target can already supply
80	    this" when it would supply someone else's software. The row is located by matching the
81	    version table's version string against the block's own `Candidate:` value rather than by
82	    the `***` marker, which points at the installed version.
83	
84	    Key and value are separable exactly as above: a name apt printed no block for gets NO
85	    key and must never be read as evidence of anything, while `Candidate: (none)` — apt
86	    knows the name and will install no version of it — gets an EMPTY SET. That distinction
87	    is what separates "the target has a candidate from the wrong place" from "the target
88	    has no candidate at all".
89	    """
90	    return _origins_by_package(policy_output, of_candidate=True)
91	
92	
93	def _origins_by_package(policy_output: str, *, of_candidate: bool) -> dict[str, frozenset[str]]:
94	    """The shared version-table walk: `{package: origin URIs of one of its version rows}`.
95	
96	    `of_candidate` picks the row — the one whose version equals the block's `Candidate:`,
97	    or the `***`-marked installed one. Everything else is identical, and duplicating the
98	    walk to vary that one predicate is what `_parse_pin_file`'s docstring records the cost
99	    of. `apt-cache policy` indents each version's origins by eight spaces as
100	    `<priority> <uri> <suite>/<component> <arch> Packages`; a block starts with an
101	    unindented `<name>:` header.
102	    """
103	    origins: dict[str, set[str]] = {}
104	    current: str | None = None
105	    candidate: str | None = None
106	    collecting = False
107	    for line in policy_output.splitlines():
108	        if line and not line[0].isspace() and line.endswith(":"):
109	            current, candidate, collecting = line[:-1], None, False
110	            origins.setdefault(current, set())
111	            continue
112	        if current is None:
113	            continue
114	        stripped = line.strip()
115	        if not stripped:
116	            continue
117	        if stripped.startswith("Candidate:"):
118	            value = stripped.removeprefix("Candidate:").strip()
119	            # `(none)` leaves `candidate` unset so no row ever matches: the key survives
120	            # with an empty set, which is not the same answer as no key at all.
121	            candidate = None if value == "(none)" else value
122	            continue
123	        if line.startswith("        "):
124	            parts = stripped.split()
125	            if collecting and len(parts) >= 2 and parts[1] != _DPKG_STATUS:
126	                origins[current].add(normalise_repo_uri(parts[1]))
127	            continue
128	        # Any other row at version-table depth opens the next version. `Installed:` and
129	        # `Version table:` land here too and match neither predicate, which closes the
130	        # previous row exactly as a real version row would.
131	        version = stripped.removeprefix("***").split()
132	        collecting = (bool(version) and version[0] == candidate) if of_candidate else stripped.startswith("***")
133	    return {name: frozenset(uris) for name, uris in origins.items()}
134	
135	
136	def packages_installed_from_no_repository(policy_output: str, queried_names: Sequence[str]) -> frozenset[str]:
137	    """The `queried_names` whose INSTALLED version comes from no configured repository —
138	    a bare `.deb` put on the machine with `dpkg --install` (D-18).
139	
140	    Callers MUST pass only names known to be installed (`apt-mark showmanual` on the
141	    machine `policy_output` came from). A name that is not installed is indistinguishable
142	    from a dpkg-only one here: neither has a repository origin for an installed version,
143	    because neither has an installed version.
144	
145	    A name apt printed NO block for is never flagged. Absence is not evidence: apt prints a
146	    block for every installed package (verified against a live `apt-mark showmanual` set),
147	    so no block means the question was not answered — an unknown name, or an `apt-cache
148	    policy` that failed outright and returned nothing. Indicting on absence would let one
149	    failed command declare a machine's entire manual set unreproducible.
150	
151	    A package hand-installed at a version NEWER than the repository's is flagged, which is
152	    correct rather than a false positive: replicating *this machine's* installed version
153	    needs the `.deb`, and the repository cannot supply it.
154	    """
155	    origins = installed_origins_by_package(policy_output)
156	    return frozenset(name for name in queried_names if name in origins and not origins[name])
